## Why signal typing comes first

Fundamental frequency, jitter, shimmer, and harmonics-to-noise ratio all
presuppose an identifiable repeating waveform. Disordered voices routinely
violate that assumption. Applying a perturbation formula to a signal that has
no periodic structure produces a number, but not a meaningful one
[@baken2000clinical]. A three-category classification of voiced signals,
originally proposed by @titze1995workshop at the NCVS Workshop on Acoustic
Voice Analysis and formalised for the clinic by @baken2000clinical, addresses
this by naming which kinds of vocal signal support which kinds of measurement.

Every measure chapter in this reference relies on the classification. This
chapter is the single authority those cross-references resolve to.

## The three types

The classification, with clinical subtypes added by @baken2000clinical shown
in italics:

### Type 1 — nearly periodic (or, in the ideal case, periodic)

Waveforms that do not undergo qualitative changes during the analysis
interval. Any modulating or subharmonic frequencies present carry energy at
least one order of magnitude below the fundamental [@baken2000clinical].

- *Subtype A*: minor random variation of F0 or waveshape.
- *Subtype B*: minor monotonic modulation — F0 or amplitude steadily
  increasing or decreasing.
- *Subtype C*: minor cyclic variation (modulation) of F0 or amplitude.

### Type 2 — organised but non-stationary

Signals with sudden qualitative changes (bifurcations), or with modulating or
subharmonic frequencies whose energy is comparable to that of the
fundamental. The signal is clearly ordered and organised, but no single F0
value validly characterises the entire segment [@baken2000clinical].

- *Subtype A*: signal bifurcation(s) present.
- *Subtype B*: F0 or amplitude discontinuity.
- *Subtype C*: large-scale modulation of F0.

### Type 3 — without apparent periodicity

Signals without apparent periodicity, and hence not validly susceptible to F0
measurement. Type 3 signals may nonetheless be chaotic in the technical
sense — carrying a covert organising principle discoverable through
dynamical-systems techniques [@baken2000clinical].

- *Subtype A*: no observable structure.
- *Subtype B*: deep-level (chaotic) organisation.

## Applying the classification

Signal typing is a visual-inspection step performed before perturbation
measurement, not a numeric procedure. The vocal waveform (or a close
correlate, such as an electroglottographic trace) is displayed and examined
for the presence of bifurcations, modulations, discontinuities, and
periodicity. The analysis window is chosen so that a single type applies
across it [@baken2000clinical]. A computer-based analysis system will happily
calculate a putative F0 for any signal, including aperiodic ones, but the
number produced has no meaning if the signal is Type 3 [@baken2000clinical].

The classification is signal-based, not disorder-based. A single speaker may
produce all three types across a session, and the same disorder can present
differently at different F0 or intensity levels. The underlying mathematical
distinction is periodicity itself: a waveform is periodic when *f*(*t* + *T*)
= *f*(*t*), so the waveform is an exact copy of itself after some period *T*
has elapsed [@titze2000principles]. Any departure from this exact-repetition
condition is aperiodicity of some kind.

## Which measures apply to which types

Signal type gates the measures that follow in Parts II–IV.

| Type | Reliable | Marginal | Unreliable / undefined |
|---|---|---|---|
| Type 1 | Jitter, shimmer, HNR, CPPS, spectral tilt, F0, all composites | — | — |
| Type 2 | CPPS, some spectral measures | HNR, spectral tilt | Jitter, shimmer, composite indices |
| Type 3 | Cepstral-domain measures (CPPS); dynamical-systems methods | — | Any measure that requires F0 tracking |

- **Perturbation measures require Type 1 signals.** For F0 evaluation to be
  meaningful, the signal should within reasonable limits be classifiable as
  Type 1, subtype A [@baken2000clinical]. Occasional discontinuities may be
  less damaging than once believed for some software [@baken2000clinical],
  but the general rule stands.
- **Noise measures (HNR, NHR) presuppose a discernible periodic component**
  to separate from the noise; they are unreliable on Type 2 and undefined on
  Type 3.
- **Cepstral peak prominence is robust across signal types.** CPP and CPPS
  do not require pitch detection or tracking and can be extracted from
  connected speech as well as sustained vowels. This is one of the practical
  reasons ASHA recommended CPP as a general dysphonia measure in preference
  to jitter, shimmer, and HNR (see the [CPPS chapter](cpps.qmd)).
- **Composite indices inherit their components' signal-type constraints.**
  Because AVQI and ABI include perturbation and HNR-like terms, they are
  sensitive to non-Type-1 material; see the [AVQI](avqi.qmd) and
  [ABI](abi.qmd) chapters.
- **Type 3 signals need dynamical-systems methods**, not periodicity-based
  measures, and that direction of investigation is one of the frontier
  areas in acoustic voice analysis [@baken2000clinical].

The practical workflow: display the signal, classify it, and if it is not
Type 1 either shorten the analysis window until a Type 1 segment is
isolated, switch to a signal-type-robust measure such as CPPS, or report the
signal as unanalyzable by perturbation methods — rather than reporting a
spurious number.

## Caveats

- The classification is human-judgment-based. Two clinicians may disagree at
  the boundaries, particularly between Type 1 subtype C and Type 2 subtype C
  (both involve F0 modulation; they differ in the magnitude relative to the
  fundamental) [@baken2000clinical].
- Software rarely refuses to compute perturbation values on non-Type-1
  signals — the user must apply the type check themselves.
- The analysis window matters. A speaker who produces Type 2 material during
  a phrase transition and Type 1 material during a sustained vowel is both,
  depending on which window is analysed.
- The Baken and Orlikoff subtypes (A, B, C) are their own extension of
  @titze1995workshop's three-type framework; other authors have used other
  subdivisions or none at all. Cite the subtype only where the sensitivity
  of the analysis warrants it.
